title: Street Medic Triage & Primary Assessment (ABCDE)
summary: A systematic protocol used by civilian first-responders and street medics during civil unrest to rapidly assess casualties and prioritize life-saving care under high-threat environments.

quick_facts.Source Work: Riot Medicine by Håkan Geijer (2020)
quick_facts.Golden Rule: Scene Safety: Medics cannot treat casualties if they become casualties themselves.
quick_facts.Triage Speed: 30 to 60 seconds per patient in mass-casualty triage.

content:
Overview & Scene Safety

Street medicine operates under austere, unpredictable conditions where conventional Emergency Medical Services (EMS) may be delayed, obstructed, or absent. The primary operational tenet is scene safety: medics evaluate kinetic hazards (police charges, tear gas canisters, stampeding crowds, hostile individuals) before approaching a casualty. If the scene becomes untenable, the medic and casualty must be relocated to a 'Warm' or 'Cold' staging zone before comprehensive treatment begins.

The ABCDE Primary Assessment Protocol

  • A — Airway (with Cervical Spine Protection): Check if the airway is clear. In unconscious trauma patients, suspect cervical spinal injury; use a jaw-thrust maneuver rather than a head-tilt chin-lift. Listen for stridor, gurgling (requires positioning on side in recovery position), or snoring.
  • B — Breathing: Assess chest rise and fall, respiratory rate, and bilateral symmetry. Look for signs of tension pneumothorax (tracheal deviation, severe shortness of breath, hyper-resonance) or flail chest from kinetic projectile strikes.
  • C — Circulation & Hemorrhage Control: Identify and immediately arrest massive external bleeding using direct pressure, wound packing, or tourniquets. Check radial pulse presence and quality (weak/thready indicates hypovolemic shock; absent radial with present carotid indicates systolic BP below ~80 mmHg).
  • D — Disability: Rapid neurological check using the AVPU scale: Alert, responds to Verbal stimuli, responds to Painful stimuli, or Unresponsive. Note pupil size, symmetry, and reactivity to light.
  • E — Exposure / Environment: Expose injuries to verify wounds while protecting the patient from hypothermia, rain, or prolonged contact with pavement.

Mass Casualty Triage: The START System

In mass casualty incidents, responders use the START algorithm. Patients who can walk are tagged Green and guided to a rally point. Non-ambulatory patients are evaluated: respiratory rate > 30/min or absent breathing until airway opened indicates Red (immediate); absent radial pulse or capillary refill > 2 sec indicates Red; inability to follow simple commands indicates Red. Patients who breathe stably and follow commands are tagged Yellow.
fiction_tips: • Sensory Details: In fiction, street triage is loud, disorienting, and claustrophobic. Describe the smell of burning rubber or tear gas mixing with copper-smelling blood, the difficulty of finding a radial pulse through thick nitrile gloves while sirens blare, and the mud-smeared knees of the medic's pants. • Common Author Mistakes: Avoid having a medic calmly perform a complex suture or IV insertion in the middle of a kinetic riot; in reality, field medicine under fire is brutal and hasty—stopping bright red arterial spurts, clearing vomitus from an airway, throwing the casualty onto a blanket drag, and sprinting into an alleyway. • Dramatic Tension: Force your medic character to make harrowing triage choices: choosing to leave a friend tagged 'Yellow' to attend to a stranger coughing pink froth tagged 'Red'.

title: Chemical Irritant Decontamination (Tear Gas CS, OC Pepper Spray)
summary: Field protocols and physiological mechanics for treating exposure to riot control agents, lacrimators (CS/CN gas), and inflammatory oleoresin capsicum (OC pepper spray).

quick_facts.Source Work: Riot Medicine by Håkan Geijer (2020)
quick_facts.Target Receptors: TRPA1 pain receptors (CS); TRPV1 thermal receptors (OC)
quick_facts.Flush Protocol: Clean cold water or 0.9% sterile saline; continuous irrigation from inner to outer canthus.
quick_facts.Field Myth Debunked: Milk / Maalox / Antacid flushes are NOT recommended (risk of bacterial infection and corneal abrasions).
quick_facts.Wind Discipline: Always approach casualties and set up staging upwind of contaminated areas.

content:
Chemical Profiles & Physiological Effects

Riot control agents are aerosolized micro-solids or liquid mists designed to incapacitate through intense irritation of mucous membranes:

  • CS Gas (2-Chlorobenzalmalononitrile): An alkylating lacrimator delivered as a pyrotechnic smoke or aerosol spray. It binds to TRPA1 ion channels on sensory nerves, producing violent blepharospasm (involuntary eye closure), burning tears, profuse rhinorrhea, coughing, chest tightness, nausea, and burning on moist skin. Symptoms peak within 20–60 seconds.
  • OC Spray (Oleoresin Capsicum): An oily resin derived from chili peppers containing capsaicin. It triggers TRPV1 heat-pain receptors, causing immediate, excruciating burning pain, temporary functional blindness from eyelid swelling, involuntary breath holding, and intense skin erythema. Because it is oil-based, it clings tenaciously to skin and fabric.

Field Decontamination Protocol

  1. Evacuate Upwind: Move the casualty into fresh, moving air. Face the casualty into the wind with eyes open and arms spread to allow air currents to blow particulates away.
  2. Dry Decontamination: Brush or blow away dry CS powder from hair and clothing before applying any liquids, as water can activate dry particulates on the skin. Carefully peel off contaminated outer layers over the head without wiping them across the eyes and nose.
  3. Eye Irrigation: Flush the eyes using copious amounts of clean, cold water or sterile physiological saline. Position the patient's head tilted toward the eye being flushed so contaminated run-off flows away from the other eye (inner canthus to outer canthus). Instruct the patient to blink repeatedly while flushing.
  4. Skin Cleansing: Wash affected skin with cold water and non-oil-based, fragrance-free soap. Hot water must be avoided because it opens skin pores and accelerates cutaneous absorption.
fiction_tips: • Sensory Details: Tear gas has a distinct odor often described by survivors as peppery, acidic, metallic, or resembling burned fruit. OC spray leaves bright yellow or orange oily stains on skin and clothing that smell of pungent, scorched peppers. • Physical Manifestations: Characters hit with CS will drool uncontrollably, spit thick strings of mucus, and experience frantic, involuntary gasping for air. Their eyelids will be swollen shut, forcing them to pry their eyelids apart with trembling fingers to see where they are running. • Tactical Reality: A character who rushes to help a friend without putting on a respirator or standing upwind will be instantly incapacitated by secondary contamination from the friend's jacket.

title: Kinetic Impact Munitions & Blunt Trauma Management
summary: Pathophysiology and emergency field stabilization of injuries caused by less-lethal kinetic projectiles including rubber-coated steel bullets, foam batons, and beanbag rounds.

quick_facts.Source Work: Riot Medicine by Håkan Geijer (2020)
quick_facts.Munition Types: Rubber-coated steel cylinders, 40mm sponge/foam-tipped rounds, 12-gauge lead-shot beanbag rounds
quick_facts.Muzzle Velocities: 60 to 100 m/s (approx. 200–330 ft/s); kinetic energies exceeding 100 Joules
quick_facts.Targeting Reality: Intended for legs/lower body; inaccurate ricochets or improper direct fire frequently strike chest, neck, and skull.
quick_facts.Deadly Complications: Depressed skull fracture, intracranial hematoma, tension pneumothorax, commotio cordis, ruptured spleen.

content:
Physics and Mechanism of Injury

Kinetic impact munitions transfer massive momentum over a short surface area upon impact. While designed to cause pain compliance without penetration, their high kinetic energy routinely produces severe blunt force trauma comparable to high-velocity sports impacts or close-range batons.

Critical Trauma Presentations

  • Head and Facial Impacts: High risk of skull fractures, concussion, traumatic brain injury (TBI), facial bone fractures (orbital blowout, broken jaw), and permanent ocular globe rupture. Any projectile strike to the head with loss of consciousness, unequal pupils, clear fluid leaking from nose/ears (CSF rhinorrhea/otorrhea), or vomiting requires immediate emergency trauma center evacuation.
  • Thoracic Trauma (Chest Strikes): Can fracture multiple ribs, producing flail chest (paradoxical movement of the chest wall during breathing) or puncturing a lung to produce a pneumothorax or hemothorax. Blunt impact directly over the cardiac silhouette during the vulnerable phase of the heartbeat can cause commotio cordis (sudden cardiac arrest).
  • Abdominal Trauma: Blunt force impacts to the left upper quadrant can lacerate or rupture the spleen; right upper quadrant impacts can damage the liver. Internal hemorrhage is characterized by rigid, distended abdomen, pale/clammy skin, rapid weak pulse, and signs of decompensating shock.

Field Stabilization Protocol

  1. Stabilize cervical spine if head or neck trauma occurred.
  2. Inspect for entrance wounds: so-called 'less-lethal' rounds can penetrate skin and lodge in tissue or muscle. Never attempt to probe or dig out an embedded projectile in the field.
  3. Apply clean sterile dressings to lacerations; apply ice or cold compresses wrapped in cloth to reduce hematoma swelling if skin is intact.
  4. Check for paradoxical chest motion and signs of tension pneumothorax (needle decompression or chest seal with one-way valve required if qualified).
fiction_tips: • Sensory Details: The impact of a 40mm sponge round or beanbag against a human rib sounds like a wet baseball bat hitting a heavy leather bag. The victim is violently knocked back, winded instantly, and often emits a strangled wheeze unable to draw breath. • The Aftermath: Bruising from kinetic rounds is not a simple blue mark; it blooms into deep plum, black, and greenish-yellow hematomas the size of dinner plates, accompanied by swelling that feels hard and feverish to the touch. • Plot Hooks: Characters shot in the torso may claim they are 'just bruised', only to collapse 30 minutes later in an alley from a slow, occult splenic rupture.

title: Severe Hemorrhage Control & Field Pressure Dressings
summary: Essential life-saving protocols for stopping severe arterial and venous hemorrhage in pre-hospital, austere, and mass-casualty environments.

quick_facts.Source Work: Riot Medicine by Håkan Geijer (2020)
quick_facts.Primary Tools: Direct pressure, hemostatic gauze (quikclot/kaolin), elastic pressure bandage (Israeli bandage), CAT tourniquet
quick_facts.Arterial vs Venous: Arterial: bright red, pulsatile/spurting, fatal blood loss in under 3 minutes. Venous: dark maroon, steady oozing flow.
quick_facts.Tourniquet Placement: High and tight on limbs (2-3 inches above bleeding site, never directly over a joint).
quick_facts.Wound Packing Rule: Pack junctional wounds (groin, axilla, base of neck) firmly into the wound cavity down to the bone.

content:
Hemorrhage Control Hierarchy

Exsanguinating hemorrhage is the leading cause of preventable trauma death. Street medics prioritize bleeding arrest before all other interventions except personal safety and patent airway obstruction.

Step-by-Step Interventions

  1. Direct Finger/Hand Pressure: Immediately press fingertips or heel of hand directly into the bleeding vessel inside the wound cavity. Lean entire body weight onto the pressure point.
  2. Wound Packing (Junctional & Deep Cavities): Tourniquets cannot be placed on the neck, groin, or armpit (junctional zones). Feed hemostatic gauze or plain sterile gauze into the wound cavity tightly, packing against the bleeding artery until the cavity is completely filled, then maintain continuous two-handed pressure for a minimum of 3 full minutes (or 5 minutes for non-hemostatic gauze).
  3. Pressure Dressing: Secure the packing with a high-tension elastic pressure bandage (such as an Israeli Emergency Bandage), wrapping firmly across the pressure bar to exert direct downward vector force over the wound site.
  4. Combat Application Tourniquet (CAT): For catastrophic extremity arterial bleeds (legs or arms), apply a windlass tourniquet 2 to 3 inches proximal to the injury (or high on the limb if clothing obscures the exact wound). Twist windlass rod until bright spurting bleeding ceases and distal pulse vanishes. Secure windlass in clip and write the application time (e.g. 'TK 14:32') on the patient's forehead or tourniquet strap with a permanent marker.
fiction_tips: • Sensory Reality: Fresh arterial blood is shockingly hot, slick, and has a heavy, metallic scent like copper pennies. It turns fabric sodden and makes fingers slip off bandages. • Author Misconceptions: Tourniquets are agonizingly painful when properly applied; a conscious character will scream from the tourniquet pressure alone, often pleading for it to be loosened. Loosening a tourniquet in the field is a fatal mistake that causes re-bleeding and releases acidic metabolic toxins. • Time Constraints: A severed femoral or brachial artery can induce irreversible hemorrhagic shock in less than 90 to 120 seconds. Characters cannot deliver lengthy speeches while bleeding out from a major limb artery.

title: Postmortem Changes: Rigor Mortis, Livor Mortis, and Algor Mortis
summary: The classical biological triad used by medicolegal death investigators and coroners to evaluate postmortem interval (PMI) and determine if a body was moved after death.

quick_facts.Source Work: NIJ Guide 308955: Death Investigation (Office of Justice Programs)
quick_facts.Rigor Mortis Onset: Noticeable in 2–4 hours (jaw/neck first), fully fixed in 8–12 hours, dissipates over 24–36 hours.
quick_facts.Livor Mortis (Lividity): Purplish discoloration in dependent areas; blanchable initially (0–6 hrs), completely fixed after 8–12 hours.
quick_facts.Algor Mortis (Cooling): Body cools toward ambient temperature at approx. 1.5°F (0.8°C) per hour under standard indoor conditions.
quick_facts.Coroner Clue: Inconsistent lividity (e.g. purple pooling on back when corpse is found face down) proves body was repositioned after death.

content:
The Physiological Triad of Death

Forensic death investigators evaluate three distinct physical processes to estimate the postmortem interval (time since death) and reconstruct the initial position and movement of the decedent:

1. Rigor Mortis (Postmortem Muscular Stiffening)

Upon death, cellular respiration halts and glycogen reserves deplete, preventing the synthesis of adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Without ATP, actin-myosin cross-bridges in muscle fibers cannot detach, locking muscles into a rigid contracture. Rigor first manifests in small muscle groups: eyelids, jaw, and neck (within 1 to 3 hours), progressing downward through the torso, arms, and legs. Peak rigidity is typically attained between 8 and 12 hours. Rigor remains fixed for roughly 12 to 24 hours, then gradually resolves as muscle proteins decompose (proteolysis), restoring flaccidity after 36 to 48 hours. If rigor is broken by manual force (e.g. moving a joint), it does not re-form.

2. Livor Mortis (Hypostasis / Postmortem Lividity)

When the heart stops pumping, gravity pulls red blood cells down into the lowest (dependent) capillaries of the body, creating reddish-purple mottling. Areas supporting pressure against hard surfaces (e.g., shoulder blades, buttocks, or tight clothing belts) remain pale and blanched because compressed capillaries cannot fill with blood.

  • Blanchable vs Fixed: During the first 4 to 6 hours, pressing a thumb against the discolored skin causes it to turn white temporarily (blanching). After 8 to 12 hours, red blood cells hemolyze and stain extravascular tissues permanently; lividity is then fixed and will not blanch.
  • Crime Scene Movement: If a decedent is discovered lying prone (face down) on a floor, but purple lividity is fixed across the back and posterior calves, the investigator knows with absolute certainty that the body lay on its back for at least 6–8 hours before being flipped over.
  • Color Variations: Cherry-red lividity indicates carbon monoxide (CO) or cyanide poisoning, or exposure to sub-freezing cold. Brownish/chocolate lividity indicates methemoglobinemia (e.g., nitrates, aniline dyes).

3. Algor Mortis (Body Cooling)

The postmortem loss of core body heat occurs primarily via conduction, convection, and radiation toward ambient room temperature. Under typical indoor temperate conditions (approx. 70°F / 21°C), a clothed adult body loses core heat at a baseline rate of approximately 1.5°F (0.8°C) per hour during the initial 12 hours. However, investigators never rely solely on liver thermometer readings: body mass, obesity, clothing layers, ambient draft, fever prior to death, and surface type heavily alter cooling rates.
fiction_tips: • Authentic Detective Dialogue: Forensic investigators rarely state a precise 'time of death' like 'he died at 10:42 PM' unless a broken wristwatch or digital timestamp confirms it. They give a window based on lividity and rigor (e.g., 'Lividity is fixed on his back and blanching is absent, but rigor hasn't resolved in the knees—we are looking at between 12 and 24 hours ago'). • The 'Moved Body' Trope: Use dual or contradictory lividity to reveal that a murder victim was transported from a secondary crime scene: 'Look at his hips. The purple pooling is on his belly, but he's slumped back against the car seat. Someone dumped him here hours after he died.' • Breaking Rigor: If a killer tries to force a rigid body into a car trunk or barrel, the sound is sickening: cracking fibrous snapping of tendons and tearing muscle fibers that leaves the broken limbs unnaturally loose.

title: Crime Scene Perimeter, Preservation & Evidence Dynamics
summary: Standard operating guidelines for securing death scenes, establishing multi-tiered perimeters, documenting scene integrity, and mitigating evidence contamination.

quick_facts.Source Work: NIJ Guide 308955: Death Investigation (Office of Justice Programs)
quick_facts.The Three Zones: Inner Core (hot scene / body location), Working Area (warm buffer / equipment), Outer Perimeter (cold zone / public & media)
quick_facts.Primary Mandate: Log Every Entry: Name, badge/title, time in, time out, reason for entry.
quick_facts.First Officer Priority: Save lives first; preserve scene second; arrest suspects third.
quick_facts.Golden Rule: Touch nothing, move nothing, use no plumbing or toilets, discard nothing inside the perimeter.

content:
The Philosophy of Scene Integrity

According to Edmond Locard's Exchange Principle, whenever two entities come into contact, a cross-transfer of physical materials occurs ('every contact leaves a trace'). The primary duty of the medicolegal death investigator (MDI) and initial responding officers is to establish physical containment before vital trace evidence (fibers, DNA, latent prints, gunshot residue, pollen) is altered or destroyed.

Establishing Concentric Perimeter Zones

  • Inner Perimeter (The Core Scene): Encompasses the body, immediate blood spatter patterns, weapon drop locations, and primary paths of ingress/egress. Access is strictly limited to the lead investigator, medical examiner/coroner, and crime scene technicians. Full PPE (nitrile gloves, shoe covers, Tyvek suits) is mandatory.
  • Working Zone (Inner Buffer): The area immediately surrounding the core scene used for staging forensic equipment, mobile lighting, and evidence packaging supplies. Superiors, detectives, and EMS staging remain here.
  • Outer Perimeter: Marked with yellow police tape at a generous perimeter (far larger than initially deemed necessary, as shrinking a perimeter is easy while expanding one after contamination is impossible). This perimeter keeps out curious patrol officers, press, family members, and the public.

Scene Security Log & Prohibitions

A uniformed officer is stationed at the single designated breach point of the outer perimeter with an Entry/Exit Log. No person enters—including chiefs of police, district attorneys, or mayors—without documenting their legal name, badge number, organization, exact timestamp in, timestamp out, and investigative purpose. Forensic technicians strictly prohibit:

  1. Using household toilets, sinks, or trash cans (may flush down DNA, drugs, or toxic substances).
  2. Using crime scene landline phones or plugging mobile chargers into outlets.
  3. Eating, drinking, smoking, or chewing tobacco anywhere within the perimeter (drops foreign ash, saliva, or food particles).
  4. Adjusting thermostats, turning on air conditioning, opening windows, or turning off lights prior to documentation.
fiction_tips: • Bureaucratic Friction: In reality, high-ranking brass, politicians, or impatient detectives often clash with meticulous forensic techs who refuse them entry without Tyvek suits and shoe booties. Use this tension to reveal character egos. • Weather Elements: Rain, snow, high wind, or summer heat are the mortal enemies of a death scene. Describe forensic techs frantically erecting pop-up tents over an outdoor body while puddles threaten to dilute tire impressions. • The Scene Log as a Plot Device: A forgotten name on the entry log or an unexplained 15-minute gap where an unauthorized person stepped inside can break an alibi or expose an insider conspiracy.

title: Differentiating Wounds: Sharp Force, Blunt Force, and Hesitation Marks
summary: Forensic criteria for distinguishing between incised wounds, stab wounds, blunt force lacerations, and suicidal hesitation marks during death investigation.

quick_facts.Source Work: NIJ Guide 308955: Death Investigation (Office of Justice Programs)
quick_facts.Stab vs Incised: Stab wound: depth into body is greater than surface length. Incised wound: surface length is greater than depth.
quick_facts.Laceration vs Cut: Lacerations (blunt force) have tissue bridging, abraded/bruised margins, and ragged edges; cuts (sharp force) have clean margins and NO tissue bridging.
quick_facts.Tissue Bridging: Intact nerve fibers, blood vessels, and connective tissue spanning the depth of the wound—pathognomonic of blunt trauma.
quick_facts.Hesitation Marks: Multiple shallow, superficial test incisions clustered parallel to a fatal deep cut; classic indicator of self-inflicted wounds.

content:
Sharp Force Trauma

Sharp force trauma results from contact with edges or points capable of dividing tissue cleanly:

  • Stab Wounds: Penetrating wounds caused by pointed instruments (knives, screwdrivers, ice picks). The depth of the tract through flesh exceeds the length of the external wound on the skin. A single-edged blade typically produces a wound with one squared/blunt extremity and one sharp/pointed extremity; a double-edged dagger produces a wound with two sharp pointed extremities.
  • Incised Wounds (Cuts): Slicing injuries caused by dragging a blade across skin. The length across the skin is longer than the wound is deep. Margins are clean, devoid of contusion (bruising), and exhibit no tissue bridging.
  • Chop Wounds: Heavy, sharp-edged weapons (axes, machetes, meat cleavers) produce deep wounds combining clean-cut edges with underlying bone grooving, comminuted fractures, and surrounding marginal contusions.

Blunt Force Trauma: Distinguishing Lacerations

Laypeople routinely call open skin wounds 'cuts,' but in forensics, a blunt force tear is a laceration. When a blunt object (pipe, baseball bat, stone, automobile bumper) impacts skin over bone (e.g. scalp, forehead), the skin splits under shear tension. Key diagnostic differentiators:

  1. Tissue Bridging: Intact elastic blood vessels, nerves, and connective tissue fibers stretch and span across the bottom of the wound cavity. Sharp knife blades sever everything cleanly; blunt impacts crush soft tissue while stronger elastic fibers remain bridged across the gap.
  2. Abraded and Contused Margins: The edges of a laceration show scrapes (abrasions) and purplish bruising (contusions) caused by the crushing impact. Sharp cuts have crisp, unbruised margins.
  3. Ragged, Irregular Edges: Lacerations have jagged, undermined edges, frequently containing foreign debris (gravel, rust, paint chips from the striking weapon).

Suicide vs Homicide Indicators: Hesitation Marks & Defense Wounds

  • Hesitation Marks: Commonly seen in suicidal sharp force deaths (wrist or throat incisions). The victim hesitates before delivering the fatal stroke, leaving several parallel, superficial scratches or shallow cuts adjacent to the deep lethal incision.
  • Defense Wounds: Found on a homicide victim's hands and forearms. Active defense wounds occur on the palms and flexor surfaces of fingers as the victim grabs the attacker's blade; passive defense wounds occur on the backs of wrists, elbows, and forearms as the victim raises arms to shield their face and chest.
fiction_tips: • Writing Plausible Medical Examiners: Have your coroner immediately correct a rookie cop who calls a head wound a 'cut': 'That's not a cut, officer. Look at the tissue bridging inside the tear and the bruised edges—he was struck with something heavy and blunt, like an iron tire iron, not sliced with a knife.' • Stab Wound Fallacy: The depth of a stab wound can actually be longer than the knife blade itself! In soft areas like the abdomen, forceful thrusting compresses fat and organs under the hilt, allowing a 4-inch blade to penetrate 5 or 6 inches deep. • Defense Wounds Narrative Impact: The presence of deep palm lacerations showing sliced tendons proves your victim fought desperately for their life before dying, changing the emotional tone of a murder revelation.

title: Forensic Chain of Custody & Evidence Packaging
summary: The legal and procedural framework governing how physical evidence is labeled, sealed, stored, and accounted for from crime scene recovery to courtroom admissibility.

quick_facts.Source Work: NIJ Guide 308955: Death Investigation (Office of Justice Programs)
quick_facts.Chain of Custody Definition: An unbroken chronological paper and digital trail accounting for the recovery, transfer, analysis, and disposition of every piece of evidence.
quick_facts.Primary Packaging Rules: Biological/wet items go in breathable PAPER bags (prevent mold/DNA degradation). Never package wet blood or clothing in airtight plastic!
quick_facts.Tamper-Evident Tape: Red or blue tamper tape sealed across bag folds, signed and dated across the boundary with permanent ink.
quick_facts.Legal Consequence: A broken chain of custody makes physical evidence inadmissible in trial, regardless of how conclusive the DNA or fingerprint match is.

content:
The Principle of Custodial Integrity

In criminal law, the court requires affirmative proof that the physical item presented before a jury is the exact item seized at the scene and that it has remained completely unaltered, uncontaminated, and untampered with. The Chain of Custody is the legal mechanism that establishes this proof.

Packaging Protocols by Evidence Type

  • Biological Evidence & Wet Clothing: Blood, semen, saliva swabs, and damp clothing from victims must never be sealed into plastic bags for storage. Moisture trapped in plastic fosters rampant microbial growth and mold, destroying cellular DNA within days. Wet items must be placed in breathable paper bags or cardboard boxes, air-dried in a climate-controlled drying locker, and repackaged in clean paper.
  • Trace Evidence & Hairs/Fibers: Small debris, paint chips, and hair samples are folded into a 'druggist fold' (pharmacist's paper packet), then placed into a labeled coin envelope to prevent electrostatic clinging or loss through seams.
  • Firearms & Weapons: Guns must be cleared (rendered safe) before packaging, with magazine removed and chamber empty. Firearm boxes utilize plastic zip-ties securing the frame without touching the bore or rifling. Never wedge a pencil or dowel down a barrel (damages barrel rifling and trace deposits).
  • Arson Debris & Volatile Accelerants: Unlike biological evidence, fire debris must be sealed immediately in airtight, clean, unlined steel paint cans or specialized nylon vapor bags to prevent volatile hydrocarbons (gasoline, kerosene fumes) from evaporating into the air.

The Evidence Tag and Seal

Every evidence package is sealed with tamper-evident tape that fractures upon attempted removal. The collecting technician writes their signature (or initials), employee badge number, and the exact date and timestamp directly across the margin where the tape meets the paper container. The accompanying tag documents:

  1. Agency case number and unique Item number (e.g. Item #04-B).
  2. Detailed description of item, including serial numbers, make, model, or color.
  3. Exact recovery location (GPS coordinates, room, distance from body).
  4. Name and title of recovering officer.
  5. Every subsequent transfer: date, releasing signature, receiving signature, and purpose (e.g., 'Transferred to State Forensics Lab for Ballistics Analysis').
fiction_tips: • Legal Drama Twist: Defense attorneys win acquittals not by disputing the science, but by finding a single signature gap in the evidence room ledger: 'Detective, who had custody of this bloodstained jacket between Tuesday at 4:00 PM and Thursday morning? Where was it kept?' • The Wet Plastic Mistake: If an inexperienced character packages bloody clothes in a ziplock bag and leaves it in a warm trunk for three days, describe the sickening, rotten stench and fuzzy greenish mold that ruined the DNA evidence. • The Break in the Seal: A villain who tampers with evidence must slice through signed tamper tape, leaving a telltale jagged white scar across the technician's inked signature.

title: Toxicity Metrics: LD50, LC50, and Dose-Response Relationships
summary: Quantitative scientific standards for measuring poison potency, lethal concentrations, therapeutic indices, and the fundamental toxicological principle that the dose makes the poison.

quick_facts.Source Work: ATSDR Toxicological Profiles Glossary (CDC / Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry)
quick_facts.Paracelsus Axiom: 'Sola dosis facit venenum' — All things are poison, and nothing is without poison; the dosage alone makes it so a thing is not a poison.
quick_facts.LD50 (Lethal Dose 50%): Milligrams of substance per kilogram of body weight (mg/kg) required to kill 50% of a test population.
quick_facts.LC50 (Lethal Concentration 50%): Concentration of a toxicant in air (ppm or mg/m³) or water that kills 50% of exposed subjects over a set duration.
quick_facts.Extremely Toxic Benchmark: Oral LD50 < 5 mg/kg (e.g. Botulinum toxin ~0.000001 mg/kg; Dioxin ~0.02 mg/kg; Potassium Cyanide ~5 mg/kg).

content:
The Dose-Response Curve

Toxicology is the science of chemical adverse effects on living organisms. Central to the field is the dose-response relationship, which dictates that biological response increases as dosage increases, typically following a sigmoidal (S-shaped) mathematical curve:

  • NOAEL (No Observed Adverse Effect Level): The highest dose of a chemical that produces no statistically significant adverse biological effects in exposed organisms.
  • LOAEL (Lowest Observed Adverse Effect Level): The lowest tested dose at which adverse effects (tremors, tissue necrosis, enzyme inhibition) are first observed.
  • LD50 (Median Lethal Dose): The statistically derived single dosage of a substance that can be expected to cause death in 50% of a given animal population. Expressed in milligrams of toxicant per kilogram of subject body mass (mg/kg). A lower LD50 indicates a vastly more lethal poison.
  • LC50 (Median Lethal Concentration): For inhaled gases, mists, or aquatic toxicants, the concentration of toxic agent in air or water (measured in parts per million [ppm] or milligrams per cubic meter [mg/m³]) that kills half the population within a specified observation window (e.g., 4-hour LC50).

Toxicity Ratings Scale

Toxicity RatingOral LD50 (Adult Human Equivalent)Examples
Practically Non-toxic> 15,000 mg/kg (Over 1 Quart)Water, sucrose
Slightly Toxic5,000 – 15,000 mg/kg (Pint to Quart)Ethanol
Moderately Toxic500 – 5,000 mg/kg (1 oz to 1 Pint)Aspirin, table salt (~3,000 mg/kg)
Very Toxic50 – 500 mg/kg (1 Teaspoon to 1 oz)Caffeine (~192 mg/kg), Nicotine (in pure state)
Extremely Toxic5 – 50 mg/kg (7 Drops to 1 Teaspoon)Potassium cyanide (~5 mg/kg), Arsenic trioxide (~15 mg/kg)
Super Toxic< 5 mg/kg (A Taste to Few Drops)Strychnine (~1 mg/kg), Ricin (~0.02 mg/kg), Botulinum toxin
fiction_tips: • Body Weight Scaling: Because LD50 is calculated in mg/kg, a poison dose that drops a 50 kg (110 lb) spy dead within 10 minutes might only cause violent nausea and delirium in a 110 kg (242 lb) bodyguard. Clever fiction writers use body mass differences to explain why an assassination failed or had unequal casualties. • The 'Instant Poison' Trope: Very few ingested poisons kill in seconds. Cyanide stops cellular respiration rapidly (within 2 to 5 minutes), but arsenic takes hours of agonizing stomach cramps, vomiting, and dehydration; thallium takes days to weeks, causing progressive hair loss, neuropathy, and organ failure. • Therapeutic Index: The difference between an effective medicine and a lethal poison is often paper-thin (e.g., digitalis/digoxin for heart failure versus cardiac arrest).

title: Routes of Chemical Exposure & Pharmacokinetics
summary: How poisons enter the human body, cross physiological membranes, distribute through organs, metabolize in the liver, and excrete through the kidneys (ADME framework).

quick_facts.Source Work: ATSDR Toxicological Profiles Glossary (CDC / Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry)
quick_facts.Fastest Route to Brain: Inhalation (seconds from alveoli into pulmonary blood, left atrium, and carotid artery).
quick_facts.First-Pass Effect: Ingested toxins are carried via portal vein directly to the liver, where hepatic enzymes may degrade or activate them.
quick_facts.Dermal Barrier: Stratum corneum (outer keratin layer of skin); lipophilic (fat-soluble) chemicals penetrate skin far faster than water-soluble ones.

content:
The ADME Framework of Toxicokinetics

Once a toxic chemical contacts an organism, its pathological progression is governed by four sequential pharmacokinetic phases: Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, and Excretion (ADME).

1. Absorption & Routes of Entry

  • Inhalation: The most rapid and dangerous systemic route of entry. The human lungs contain over 100 square meters of alveolar surface area separated from bloodstream capillary networks by an ultra-thin cellular membrane (less than 1 micron). Inhaled gases (carbon monoxide, hydrogen cyanide) and fine aerosols bypass the liver entirely, entering the carotid arteries to bathe the brain in seconds.
  • Ingestion (Oral): Toxins absorbed in the stomach and small intestine enter the portal venous system, traveling directly to the liver before reaching systemic circulation. This first-pass metabolism allows hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes to detoxify certain agents—or catastrophically bioactivate non-toxic prodrugs into deadly metabolites (e.g., acetaminophen overdose creating toxic NAPQI). Food in the stomach delays gastric emptying and buffers absorption.
  • Dermal (Cutaneous): The stratum corneum is a formidable physical barrier against water-soluble (hydrophilic) compounds. However, lipid-soluble (lipophilic) compounds—such as organophosphate nerve agents (VX, sarin), nicotine, and aniline dyes—penetrate intact skin effortlessly and silently, producing delayed toxicity without skin burns.
  • Injection (Parenteral): Intravenous (IV) delivers 100% bioavailability immediately into the bloodstream. Intramuscular (IM) and subcutaneous routes are slower, dependent on local capillary perfusion.

2. Distribution & Target Organs

Once absorbed into systemic circulation, toxicants distribute according to blood flow and tissue affinity. Highly perfused organs (brain, heart, kidneys, liver) receive the toxic payload first. Lipid-soluble poisons readily cross the protective blood-brain barrier, while heavy metals (lead, cadmium) accumulate in bone and renal tubules.

3. Excretion

The kidneys are the primary elimination route for water-soluble metabolites via urine. Volatile compounds (ethanol, acetone) are exhaled through the lungs, while heavy molecular weight compounds are excreted via bile into feces.
fiction_tips: • Assassination Tactics: A poison that must be swallowed can be detected by taste or smell; an invisible lipophilic poison applied to a doorknob or steering wheel (dermal absorption) allows the assassin to be miles away before symptoms strike. • The Breath Clue: Inhaled or metabolically volatile poisons betray themselves on the victim's breath: cyanide smells faintly of bitter almonds (though 20–40% of humans carry a genetic inability to smell it); arsenic produces a distinct garlic breath odor; organophosphates smell of rotten onions or garlic. • Antidote Timing: Because inhaled toxins reach the brain in seconds, antidotes (such as amyl nitrite inhalants or auto-injectors) must be administered immediately, whereas food-borne toxins allow time for gastric lavage or activated charcoal administration.

title: Bioaccumulation, Biological Half-Life & Chronic Poisoning
summary: Mechanisms of cumulative toxicity where toxins build up in fatty tissues, bone, and organs faster than the body can eliminate them, creating slow, insidious illness.

quick_facts.Source Work: ATSDR Toxicological Profiles Glossary (CDC / Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry)
quick_facts.Biological Half-Life (t½): The time required for half the quantity of an administered substance to be naturally metabolized and eliminated from the body.
quick_facts.Classic Bioaccumulators: Lead (stored in bone for decades), Mercury (crosses blood-brain barrier), Cadmium (kidney cortex), Polychlorinated biphenyls (adipose tissue).
quick_facts.Mees' Lines: Transverse white bands across fingernails caused by chronic arsenic poisoning episodes.
quick_facts.Mad Hatter Syndrome: Erethism mercurialis (chronic mercury toxicity from hat felting: personality changes, extreme shyness, tremors, paranoia).

content:
Acute vs Chronic Poisoning Dynamics

Toxicological profiles distinguish sharply between acute single-dose poisoning and chronic low-dose exposure:

  • Acute Exposure: Contact with a chemical for less than 14 days (typically a single massive dose). Characterized by rapid onset of dramatic physiological collapse: convulsions, respiratory arrest, cardiac arrhythmias, or corrosive gastrointestinal burning.
  • Chronic Exposure: Repeated exposure to low doses of a toxicant over months, years, or decades. The daily dose may be completely asymptomatic on its own, but if the chemical's biological half-life exceeds the elimination rate, the toxicant bioaccumulates in anatomical reservoirs until a toxic threshold is breached.

Heavy Metal Tissue Sequestration
